zones.what: Exterior photos of the hull show large white lifeboat/tender housings spanning three guest decks (8, 9, 10) on both sides midship; Royal Caribbean flags some of these cabins with a stated percentage obstruction (e.g. one guest's travel agent was told cabin 8564 carried a 20% obstruction).
zones.effect: The view straight down toward the water is blocked by the boat itself, though the open horizon above the boat line remains visible; deck 8 sits most directly at the boat line so it is generally the worst-affected, with 9 and 10 progressively less blocked.
zones.mattersTo: Matters to photographers/view-focused cruisers and to anyone who booked expecting a completely clear balcony rail-to-water view; does not matter much to guests who mainly want fresh air, horizon, and sunlight, which are largely preserved.
zones.source: boards.cruisecritic.com thread on 'Icon of the Seas cabins with 20% obstruction' describing 3 lifeboat-marked decks (8,9,10); confirmed as a real, cruise-line-labeled obstruction type in a Fodor's forum thread where a poster changed cabins after being told theirs had 'lifeboat obstruction.'

zones.what: Infinite Central Park View Balcony cabins on deck 10 midship (e.g. cabin 10225) sit directly above a large entrance structure to the Royal Promenade (the 'Pearl' installation), which occupies much of the view straight down into Central Park.
zones.effect: A first-hand review reported the obstruction was not disclosed at booking and meaningfully blocked the intended park view from the room.
zones.mattersTo: Matters to buyers of Central Park-facing infinite balconies who want an unobstructed park view; less relevant to guests who just want the indoor/outdoor infinite-balcony feature itself.
zones.source: royalcaribbeanblog.com first-hand review: 'Because my cabin was located right above The Pearl, my view was partially obstructed... My cabin was not labeled as obstructed online.'

zones.what: Deck 14 forward/midship cabins sit directly beneath the Chill Island pool deck (deck 15), where crew move and stack lounge chairs early morning and late at night.
zones.effect: Guests report being woken by chair-scraping noise around or before 6am and hearing pool activity/music during the day.
zones.mattersTo: Matters to light sleepers and anyone wanting to sleep in; less relevant to guests who plan to be up early anyway or who value proximity to the pool deck.
zones.source: royalcaribbeanblog.com 'cabins to avoid': 'being directly below the pool deck can be noisy... crew members shuffling chairs around the pool deck very early in the morning'; corroborated by CruiseCritic editor review.

zones.what: Aft cabins on deck 14 sit beneath both The Hideaway adults-only pool/bar and, adjacent to it, the Windjammer buffet (deck 15).
zones.effect: A first-hand account reported DJ music from The Hideaway blasting through most sea days and separately, heavy early-morning foot traffic/noise from Windjammer buffet operations overhead.
zones.mattersTo: Matters to light sleepers or anyone avoiding daytime noise; less relevant to guests who want to be near the adult pool scene or grab-and-go breakfast.
zones.source: royalcaribbeanblog.com: 'I would avoid booking any cabins at the aft of the ship on deck 14 since these are located below The Hideaway... these aft cabins are directly under the Windjammer.'

zones.what: Far-forward cabins on decks 12 and 14 sit near/below the AquaDome, which hosts evening aqua-acrobatic shows with amplified bass music.
zones.effect: Light sleepers may pick up thumping bass on show nights; RoyalCaribbeanBlog notes shows run only a handful of times per cruise, so it is not a constant nightly issue.
zones.mattersTo: Matters to light sleepers on show nights; not a concern for most cruisers most nights.
zones.source: cruisecritic.com editor review: 'cabins far forward on Deck 12 or Deck 14... pick up some noise from the AquaDome – mostly bass'; royalcaribbeanblog.com corroborates with same forward-deck-12/14 claim.

zones.what: Oceanview/Interior cabins around numbers 4156–4670 sit near the two-deck Music Hall nightclub and the Absolute Zero ice-skating arena/theater (decks 4–5), and the Royal Theater also spans decks 4–5 forward.
zones.effect: Forward cabins near these decks-4–6 entertainment venues get post-show hallway crowds and, per one listicle, complaints about noise near the Royal Theater and Attic comedy club.
zones.mattersTo: Matters to light sleepers and families with early bedtimes; irrelevant to night owls who'll be at the shows anyway.
zones.source: cruisemapper.com deck-4 plan lists cabins 4156–4670 as Oceanview/Interior adjacent to Absolute Zero and Music Hall; cruisecritic.com notes Royal Theater 'spans decks 4 and 5 on the forward end of the ship.'

zones.what: Icon-class ships use 22 'destination' elevators grouped into forward and aft atrium banks rather than scattered midship banks, with digital panels assigning guests to a car before boarding so cars make fewer stops.
zones.effect: This concentrates elevator traffic (and associated door-ding/hallway noise) tightly around the forward and aft atrium zones rather than spreading it along the whole corridor, so cabins right next to those two atrium banks get the most 24/7 traffic while cabins between them are quieter.
zones.mattersTo: Matters to light sleepers booking cabins immediately adjacent to either atrium; matters positively to guests who want fast, low-wait vertical access.
zones.source: cruisemapper.com: '22 destination elevators (located in the forward and aft atriums)... digital panels before boarding... fewer stops along the way'; worldofcruising.co.uk confirms elevators are 'positioned in the forward and aft atriums.'

zones.what: A bow-to-stern crew corridor nicknamed 'I-95' runs on the lowest decks, lined with crew cabins, staff dining, and access points into machinery spaces; on Icon/Oasis-class ships this network is described as unusually large given the scale of the crew complement (2,350).
zones.effect: Guest cabins on the lowest passenger decks (3–4) sitting above this corridor may be closer to crew movement and service-elevator activity than upper decks, though the corridor itself is not guest-accessible.
zones.mattersTo: Matters mainly to guests booking the lowest-numbered guest cabins who are sensitive to any residual footstep/service noise from below; not a concern for mid-to-upper deck cabins.
zones.source: thetravel.com: crew corridor 'I-95'... 'On mega ships such as Royal Caribbean's Icon Class or Oasis Class vessels, the corridor is massive, reflecting the need to serve over 7,000 passengers.'

zones.what: A guest in an aft-facing stateroom on deck 12 reported vibration that was absent for the first five days of a cruise and then became pronounced enough to 'literally shake the cabin non stop.'
zones.effect: Vibration in aft cabins can be intermittent rather than constant, possibly tied to speed/heading changes, but when present it is strong enough to be a comfort complaint even fairly high up the ship (deck 12).
zones.mattersTo: Matters to light sleepers and anyone sensitive to vibration booking aft cabins, even on mid-to-upper decks, not just the lowest aft decks.
zones.source: royalcaribbeanblog.com forum post 'Icon: Excessive vibration deck 12 aft': 'the vibrations have become very pronounced and literally shake the cabin non stop.'

zones.what: Forward cabins are noted to experience anchor-chain noise during port-morning anchoring/mooring operations.
zones.effect: Guests in forward cabins on the lower decks can be woken by chain noise on port-arrival mornings.
zones.mattersTo: Matters to light sleepers who prefer to sleep past early port arrivals; less relevant to guests planning to be up early for excursions anyway.
zones.source: about2cruise.co.uk Icon of the Seas cabin guide: 'Forward rooms may have anchor noise during port arrivals.'

zones.what: Most of Icon's top-tier suites (Grand Suites, Owner's Suites, Sky/Panoramic Suites, Royal/Icon Loft Suites) are clustered forward on decks 16–18, the highest and farthest-forward guest decks on the ship.
zones.effect: This combination of high-deck-plus-far-forward placement is repeatedly flagged as the worst spot for motion sensitivity on this class, despite the ship's stabilizer technology.
zones.mattersTo: Matters greatly to motion-sensitive suite shoppers who may want to trade the forward suite view for a midship or aft one; irrelevant to guests unaffected by motion.
zones.source: cruisemummy.co.uk: 'Many of the top suites on Icon of the Seas are situated on Decks 16, 17 and 18, right at the front of the ship. That's the worst area you could be in if you feel seasick.'

zones.what: Royal Caribbean Blog and Cruise Critic both advise that despite Icon's stabilizers, the ship still noticeably moves in rough seas, and that midship cabins (including many of the new Infinite Balcony cabins) feel the least motion.
zones.effect: Midship cabins on lower-to-mid decks are the recommended, lowest-motion choice class-wide; forward and aft extremes on any deck feel more sway.
zones.mattersTo: Matters to any motion-sensitive guest choosing between forward, midship, and aft on this very long (365m) ship.
zones.source: royalcaribbeanblog.com: 'those who are prone to seasickness should prioritize cabins located midship. Many of the new infinite cabins onboard Icon of the Seas are located midship'; cruisecritic.com corroborates ship still moves when rough.

zones.what: Icon-class Infinite Balcony cabins that face inward onto Central Park or Surfside have no solid balcony privacy divider from the cabins directly across the atrium-like neighborhood, unlike a traditional side balcony.
zones.effect: Guests must lower the window shade for privacy, which then removes the view/daylight entirely — reviewers explicitly contrast this unfavorably with a traditional balcony that keeps some privacy via drapes while the outdoor space stays usable.
zones.mattersTo: Matters to guests booking Central Park/Surfside-view Infinite Balconies who value being able to sit outside without being seen; does not matter to guests who plan to keep the shade down anyway or who booked for the neighborhood view rather than privacy.
zones.source: cruiseline.com: 'all the cabins across from you can see directly into your cabin and vice versa. You have to lower your window shade for privacy... no view and no daylight.'

zones.what: Icon and Star of the Seas replaced the traditional flimsy interior connecting door between connecting cabins with two separate exterior (hallway-facing) doors that can each be locked independently.
zones.effect: This is reported to meaningfully reduce the classic connecting-cabin noise/privacy complaint (thin shared interior door) versus older Royal Caribbean ship classes.
zones.mattersTo: Matters positively to families/groups booking connecting cabins on this class; a genuine class-specific improvement not present on older sister-line ships.
zones.source: nationaltoday.com / royalcaribbeanblog.com: Icon and Star of the Seas 'feature exterior doors to connecting cabins — replacing the traditional interior door,' addressing sound/privacy complaints.

leads.source: cruisesnooze.com and cruisegalore.com 'cabins to avoid' listicles (ranges differ between the two sources)

leads.source: cruisemummy.co.uk Icon of the Seas cabins guide

leads.claim: These cabins sit adjacent to the Absolute Zero ice arena and the two-level Music Hall nightclub on deck 4, both nightly entertainment/music venues.

unknowns: Whether Icon-class hulls have a genuine cantilevered 'hump' balcony feature (as on Oasis-class ships); the only 'hump' text found was boilerplate on an aggregator's Wonder of the Seas (Oasis-class) page and did not appear on that same aggregator's Icon of the Seas deck pages — treated as boilerplate and excluded rather than assumed.

Whether the highest forward suite decks (16-18) sit atop an inward hull taper that hides the straight-down view while preserving the horizon — no ship-specific source confirming a taper effect was found for Icon class.

Exact cabin-number ranges and percentages that Royal Caribbean's own deck-plan tool flags as lifeboat-obstructed on decks 8, 9, and 10 (confirmed the line does label some cabins, but the specific ranges/percentages beyond cabin 8564 were not found).

Whether bow-thruster noise is a distinct, reported issue for very-forward lower-deck cabins on this class specifically (no ship-specific first-hand account found, only generic forward-cabin anchor/motion commentary).
